title.en: Horses' Hoofs: Poh Loh the Horse-Breaker (Zhuangzi)

region.en: The horse-pastures (symbolic pin: Zhangye, Gansu, China)
region.zh: 馬牧之野（象徵定位：甘肅張掖）

texts.period: Zhuangzi ch. 9, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 9

summary.en: Horses have hoofs to carry them over frost and snow, and hair against the wind — palatial dwellings are of no use to them. Then Poh Loh appeared saying he understood the management of horses: he branded, clipped, halted, shackled and starved them until more than half died; and bridled and bitted, the horses learn to resist and bite — their natures become depraved, the fault of Poh Loh.
summary.zh: 馬蹄可以踐霜雪，毛可以禦風寒；及至伯樂曰我善治馬，燒之剔之，刻之雒之，饑之渴之，馬之死者已過半矣。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Horses have hoofs to carry them over frost and snow; hair, to protect them from wind and cold. They eat grass and drink water, and fling up their heels over the champaign. Such is the real nature of horses. Palatial dwellings are of no use to them.

One day Poh Loh appeared, saying, "I understand the management of horses." So he branded them, and clipped them, and pared their hoofs, and put halters on them, tying them up by the head and shackling them by the feet, and disposing them in stables, with the result that two or three in every ten died. Then he kept them hungry and thirsty, trotting them and galloping them, and grooming, and trimming, with the misery of the tasselled bridle before and the fear of the knotted whip behind, until more than half of them were dead.

Horses live on dry land, eat grass and drink water. When pleased, they rub their necks together. When angry, they turn around and kick up their heels at each other. Thus far only do their natural dispositions carry them. But bridled and bitted, with a plate of metal on their foreheads, they learn to cast vicious looks, to turn the head to bite, to resist, to get the bit out of the mouth or the bridle into it. And thus their natures become depraved,--the fault of Poh Loh.

title.en: The Strong Thief Carries Off the Till: T'ien Ch'êng Tzŭ Steals Ch'i (Zhuangzi)

region.en: The State of Ch'i (Linzi, Shandong, China)

texts.period: Zhuangzi ch. 10, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 10

summary.en: Locks and cords protect trunks from small thieves; a strong thief carries off the till with box and bag, his only fear being that the locks are not strong enough. So T'ien Ch'êng Tzŭ slew the Prince of Ch'i and stole not only his kingdom but the wisdom-tricks of the Sages as well — and for twelve generations his descendants ruled, while the small States did not dare to blame him.
summary.zh: 為之斗斛以量之，則並與斗斛而竊之；為之仁義以矯之，則並與仁義而竊之。田成子一朝殺齊君而盜其國，所盜者豈獨其國邪？並與其聖知之法而盜之。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: The precautions taken against thieves who open trunks, search bags, or ransack tills, consist of securing with cords and fastening with bolts and locks. This is what the world calls wit. But a strong thief comes who carries off the till on his shoulders, with box and bag to boot. And his only fear is that the cords and locks should not be strong enough!

And within its four boundaries not a temple or shrine was dedicated, nor a district or hamlet governed, but in accordance with the rules laid down by the Sages. Yet one morning T'ien Ch'êng Tzŭ slew the Prince of Ch'i, and stole his kingdom. And not his kingdom only, but the wisdom-tricks which he had got from the Sages as well; so that although T'ien Ch'êng Tzŭ acquired the reputation of a thief, he lived as comfortably as ever did either Yao or Shun. The small States did not venture to blame, nor the great States to punish him; and so for twelve generations his descendants ruled over Ch'i.

One man steals a purse, and is punished. Another steals a State, and becomes a Prince. But charity and duty to one's neighbour are integral parts of princedom. Does he not then steal charity and duty to one's neighbour together with the wisdom of the Sages?

title.en: Robber Chê and the Tao of Thieving (Zhuangzi)

region.en: Robber Chê's mountain fastness (symbolic pin: Mount T'ai, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 盜跖之山寨（象徵定位：山東泰山）

texts.period: Zhuangzi ch. 10, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 10

summary.en: An apprentice asks Robber Chê whether there is Tao in thieving. Pray tell me of something in which there is not, he answers — the wisdom to locate booty, the courage to go in first, the heroism to come out last, the shrewdness to calculate success, the justice to divide the spoil equally; there has never yet been a great robber without these five. It was the appearance of Sages that caused the appearance of great robbers.
summary.zh: 跖之徒問於跖曰：盜亦有道乎？跖曰：何適而無有道邪——妄意室中之藏，聖也；入先，勇也；出後，義也；知可否，知也；分均，仁也。聖人不死，大盜不止。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); Robber Chê is Zhuangzi's trickster foil to Confucian virtue. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: An apprentice to Robber Chê asked him saying, "Is there then TAO in thieving?" "Pray tell me of something in which there is not TAO," Chê replied. "There is the wisdom by which booty is located. The courage to go in first, and the heroism of coming out last. There is the shrewdness of calculating success, and justice in the equal division of the spoil. There has never yet been, a great robber who was not possessed of these five."

Drive out the Sages and leave the robbers alone,--then only will the empire be governed. As when the stream ceases the gully dries up, and when the hill is levelled the chasm is filled; so when Sages are extinct, there will be no more robbers, but the empire will rest in peace.

title.en: The Golden Age of Knotted Cords (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 結繩而用之：至德之世（莊子）

region.en: The age of Yung Ch'êng, Ta T'ing, and Shên Nung (symbolic pin: Song, Henan, China)
region.zh: 容成氏、大庭氏、神農之世（象徵定位：宋，今河南）

texts.period: Zhuangzi ch. 10, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 10

summary.en: In the Golden Age of the ancient rulers the people used knotted cords, were content with what food and raiment they could get, and lived simple and peaceful lives. Neighbouring districts were within sight, the cocks and dogs of one could be heard in the other — yet the people grew old and died without ever interchanging visits. In those days, government was indeed perfect.
summary.zh: 昔者容成氏、大庭氏、伯皇氏、中央氏、栗陸氏、驪畜氏、軒轅氏、赫胥氏、尊盧氏、祝融氏、伏羲氏、神農氏——當是時也，民結繩而用之，甘其食，美其服，鄰國相望，雞狗之音相聞，民至老死而不相往來。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the Taoist Golden Age (parallel to the mythic first world). Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: Have you never heard of the Golden Age, the days of Yung Ch'êng, Ta T'ing, Poh Huang, Chung Yang, Li Lu, Li Hsü, Hsien Yüan, Hê Hsü, Tsun Lu, Chu Yung, Fu Hsi, and Shên Nung? Then the people used knotted cords.

They were contented with what food and raiment they could get. They lived simple and peaceful lives. Neighbouring districts were within sight, and the cocks and dogs of one could be heard in the other, yet the people grew old and died without ever interchanging visits. In those days, government was indeed perfect.
